prompt.context: Your client is a medical device company. Recently they acquired a company that produces heart stents. Heart stents are small devices that keep arteries propped open during open heart surgery; they are left in afterwards to prevent the arteries from collapsing. Alternatives to heart stents are drugs or not using anything. The CEO feels that the previous management had not maximized the market potential for these heart stents.
prompt.question: He has asked you to determine what the potential market size is as well as determine the best method to distribute the product.

clarifying_info.q: Who needs heart stents? What is the incidence rate?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 1% of people over the age of 55 will need open heart surgery in any given year.

clarifying_info.q: Are heart stents superior to alternatives?
clarifying_info.a: Heart stents are more effective than other alternatives (drugs or nothing).
All insurance, including Medicare/Medicaid, will cover heart stents.
Only cardiologists and cardio-surgeons perform the surgery where heart stents would be used.
There are two other companies that produce heart stents, but our client is the clear market leader with over 50% of the market today.
There are three options: (1) use the current proprietary sales force, (2) create a distinct new sales force for heart stents, or (3) use medical distributors.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profile of the current sales force?
clarifying_info.a: The current sales force is comprised primarily of pharmaceutical-style sales reps with little or no medical training.

clarifying_info.q: What do other heart stent manufacturers do for distribution?
clarifying_info.a: Other heart stent manufacturers use distributors.

clarifying_info.q: What would a new distinct sales force look like?
clarifying_info.a: It would be comprised of surgeons who would perform a heart surgery alongside a cardiologist and demonstrate how to use the heart stents. It is not a problem to hire qualified sales reps for a new sales force.

exhibits.shows: A comparison table of three distribution options (Current Sales Force, New Sales Force, Distributors) across three dimensions: Cost, Effectiveness, and Other considerations.
exhibits.data: Rows: Cost, Effectiveness, Other. Columns: Current Sales Force, New Sales Force, Distributors.

framework: Market sizing: estimate the number of heart stents needed per year (US then global)
Competitive analysis: assess market share and positioning
Distribution channel evaluation: compare current sales force, new dedicated sales force, and medical distributors on cost, effectiveness, and other factors
Recommendation: select the best distribution channel with rationale and caveats

questions.prompt: What is the US market size for heart stents per year?
questions.guidance: Segment the US population by age, isolate the 55+ cohort, apply the 1% surgery rate. Strong answer uses clean round numbers and shows the arithmetic explicitly.

math.setup: US population ~300M. Divide into three equal age cohorts: 0-25, 25-55, 55+. Apply 1% surgery rate to the 55+ cohort.
steps: 100M x 1% = 1M heart stents needed per year in the US
math.answer: ~1 million heart stent procedures per year in the US

questions.prompt: What is the global (world) market size?
questions.guidance: Candidate should extend to developed countries with advanced healthcare. A reasonable assumption is that global volume is roughly 3-4x the US.

math.setup: Assume other developed countries with advanced healthcare represent approximately 3x the US market.
math.answer: ~4 million heart stent procedures per year globally

questions.prompt: How should the company distribute heart stents? Compare the three options.
questions.guidance: A strong answer structures the comparison across cost, effectiveness, and other qualitative factors for all three options, then makes a clear recommendation with caveats.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the pros and cons of each distribution option?

categories.name: Current Sales Force
ideas: Requires hiring additional reps to handle new product line
Mix of fixed and variable costs — middle cost option
Sales reps are pharmaceutical-style, not medically trained — not suited for in-depth product consultation or demonstration
Already have existing relationships with hospitals

categories.name: New Dedicated Sales Force (Surgeons)
ideas: Most expensive option due to large fixed costs with some variable
Most effective channel — surgeon reps can demonstrate the product in the OR alongside cardiologists
Need to build new relationships with doctors and hospitals — takes time
Current sales force may resent the higher-paid new sales force

categories.name: Medical Distributors
ideas: Purely variable costs — most cost-effective for small or new markets where sales are unpredictable
Distributors already have relationships with doctors and hospitals
Also sell competitor products — may not prioritize our product
May not be able to demonstrate the product properly

recommendation: Recommend building a new dedicated sales force comprised of surgeons as the primary long-term distribution channel, given the product's technical complexity and the need for in-OR demonstration to drive adoption among cardiologists

For new or small markets (e.g., emerging markets like Peru or Singapore where sales volumes are unpredictable and no existing relationships exist), use distributors initially as a low-risk, variable-cost entry point
risks: High upfront fixed costs and time required to build the new sales force
Potential internal friction if existing sales reps resent the higher-paid new team
Distributors also carry competitor products and may not champion our stents
next_steps: Quantify the cost of building the new sales force versus projected revenue uplift
Map existing hospital and cardiologist relationships to identify quick wins
Develop a transition plan for current sales reps covering non-stent products
Pilot the new sales force in one or two high-volume markets before full rollout
